task.title:
We are continuing the EXISTING ThirdEye AI hackathon project. Your task is to COMPLETE the end-to-end IBM Bob integration so that IBM Bob's role in the application is unmistakable, functional, and easy to demonstrate to hackathon judges.

This is an implementation task, NOT merely an audit or report. Inspect the existing code first, then implement and validate the missing integration pieces in this task.

WORKSPACE:
You are currently in the existing thirdeye-backend workspace. The project also has an existing separate React/Vite frontend workspace. Inspect the available workspace and related files. If the frontend workspace is accessible, make coordinated changes there when necessary. If it is not accessible, complete the backend/MCP work that can safely be done, and provide exact frontend changes or steps still required. Do not pretend to have modified inaccessible files.

CURRENT VERIFIED PROJECT STATE:
- ThirdEye AI has an existing Spring Boot backend, React/Vite frontend, and MCP server.
- The existing MCP server is named thirdeye and is connected in IBM Bob. Review-related tools are visible.
- The Findings page works and displays the SQL Injection Test 3 result for the Lost & Found repository: a High severity finding in UserService.java, line 2.
- The existing backend review pipeline and test generation contain deterministic/mock functionality. Do not misrepresent mock output as real LLM-powered analysis.
- The project is approximately 70% complete.
- Existing API endpoints, review pipeline, findings, UI, and MCP implementation must be preserved wherever they work.

PRIMARY GOAL:
Make IBM Bob a genuine, visible, end-to-end integration in ThirdEye AI. A judge should be able to see how Bob interacts with ThirdEye, uses its tools, retrieves real project/review data, assists with code review and test generation, and returns useful results through a clearly demonstrable workflow.

A successful result must be more than an MCP server being connected. Implement the actual missing integration and user-facing demonstration experience, while distinguishing Bob's real tool usage from any deterministic backend analysis.

NON-NEGOTIABLE BUDGET AND PRESERVATION RULES:
1. Inspect the existing implementation and reuse it. Do not recreate the project, rebuild working components, or perform broad refactoring.
2. Make one coordinated, focused implementation using the existing architecture, MCP server, Spring Boot APIs, and React frontend.
3. Do not repeat SQL Injection Test 3 or create duplicate reviews/findings. Use its existing result as the initial read-only integration test.
4. Do not perform unnecessary broad scans, repeated model calls, or separate subtasks. Keep all related integration changes in this task.
5. Do not add a new LLM provider, paid API, or external service. Do not require new API credentials or paid infrastructure unless the existing project already has them configured and the requirements support their use.
6. Do not install dependencies or replace libraries unless essential. Prefer existing dependencies and patterns.
7. Do not expose secrets, API keys, credentials, environment variables, or private configuration in frontend code, logs, screenshots, or demo output.
8. Do not claim Bob invoked a tool, performed analysis, generated tests, or completed an integration unless it was actually executed and verified.
9. Preserve existing API contracts, authentication/security behavior, working UI, database entities, and data. Avoid breaking changes.
10. If a requirement cannot be completed because of missing workspace access, credentials, or Bob runtime limitations, implement the safe parts and clearly identify the precise blocker. Do not silently substitute a fake integration.

PHASE 1 — INSPECT AND UNDERSTAND EXISTING CODE
Inspect only the relevant existing files and components:
- MCP server entry point, registered tool definitions, tool handlers, and backend API calls.
- MCP configuration and transport used to connect Bob.
- Existing project, review, findings, diff, and test-generation APIs.
- Existing React pages and API service layer, particularly the Findings, Overview, Report, and Tests pages.
- Existing environment/configuration and tests relevant to the integration.

Use actual tool names, actual endpoint paths, and actual data models from the repository. Do not invent API contracts or duplicate existing MCP tools.

Identify the minimum set of missing pieces required to make the complete Bob workflow demonstrable.

PHASE 2 — MAKE THE BOB-TO-THIRDEYE MCP WORKFLOW GENUINELY FUNCTIONAL
Complete and verify the existing MCP integration so Bob can use the existing ThirdEye backend tools.

Required capabilities, using existing tools where available:
- Discover and list ThirdEye projects.
- Retrieve a selected project and its existing reviews.
- Retrieve review status, summary, findings, evidence, and code diff.
- Initiate a new review through an existing supported operation when requested.
- Retrieve test-generation results and initiate test generation where supported.
- Return structured, understandable tool responses and meaningful errors.
- Handle unavailable backend/API connections without fabricating success.
- Avoid duplicate operations and respect existing idempotency behavior.

Verify read-only access first using the EXISTING Lost & Found SQL Injection Test 3 review and findings. Do not create another copy of that review.

Then verify at least one genuine Bob-to-MCP-to-backend workflow using the connected tools, if the runtime supports invoking them. Record the actual calls and results.

If a Bob runtime tool invocation cannot be executed in this environment, do not claim it worked. Complete the integration code that can be validated and explain exactly which manual Bob action remains.

PHASE 3 — CREATE A CLEAR, JUDGE-FRIENDLY BOB EXPERIENCE IN THE EXISTING FRONTEND
Inspect the existing frontend before making changes.

Add or complete a dedicated, polished IBM Bob integration experience within the existing ThirdEye UI, using the current design system and routing conventions. Do not redesign the entire app.

A judge should immediately understand:
- What IBM Bob does in ThirdEye.
- Which actions are performed by Bob through the MCP integration.
- Which operations are handled by the existing ThirdEye backend.
- What data is retrieved from the actual backend.
- How the user can run and observe a complete demonstration.

The experience should provide a clear entry point, such as an IBM Bob Integration or Bob Assistant section, using the existing navigation patterns.

Where supported by the existing runtime, provide a practical workflow for:
1. Selecting an existing project and review.
2. Asking Bob to retrieve and explain the review and findings through MCP.
3. Viewing actual returned findings, evidence, and recommendations in ThirdEye.
4. Requesting test-generation results through the existing tool/API workflow.
5. Displaying operation status, results, errors, and provenance.

Do not build a fake chat interface that merely displays hardcoded responses and claims Bob is connected. Do not embed private credentials or expose the Bob account's internal data.

If the Bob chat itself cannot be embedded or controlled through an officially supported interface, do not invent an unofficial integration. Instead, create a clearly labelled Bob integration launch/instructions panel inside ThirdEye that guides the user through the real connected Bob MCP workflow. Show actual backend data separately from Bob-generated explanations, and clearly indicate which steps require interaction in IBM Bob.

Do not present a static mockup as a functioning integration. Any demo data or simulated response must be visibly labelled as such.

PHASE 4 — MAKE THE DEMO END-TO-END AND REPRODUCIBLE
Create a concise, reproducible demonstration flow using the existing project data.

Preferred demonstration:
1. Open ThirdEye AI and navigate to the IBM Bob integration experience.
2. Show that the thirdeye MCP server is connected in IBM Bob.
3. Ask Bob to retrieve the existing Lost & Found project and SQL Injection Test 3 review.
4. Have Bob retrieve the actual findings through MCP and explain the High severity SQL injection finding.
5. Show the returned information in ThirdEye and identify its source.
6. Demonstrate test generation through the existing supported tools, if safe and available.
7. Show the difference between Bob's explanation, backend findings, and deterministic/mock engine output.

Do not rerun the existing review simply to create demo content.

Make sure the demo does not depend on a judge having access to this particular Bob account or any private credentials. Explain any setup needed for a fresh authorized environment.

PHASE 5 — TEST AND VALIDATE
After implementation:
- Run relevant existing backend tests and build checks.
- Run relevant MCP compilation/tests if the existing setup supports them.
- Run frontend build/lint/tests where available.
- Validate API endpoint mappings and error handling.
- Verify that existing functionality has not been unnecessarily removed or changed.
- Test the new integration workflow using real tool responses wherever the environment permits.
- Report the actual commands/results and distinguish executed tests from checks that could not be run.

Do not spend time rewriting unrelated tests or resolving unrelated pre-existing warnings unless they block this integration.

FINAL REPORT REQUIRED:
At completion, provide:
1. Exact files changed and what was implemented.
2. The complete Bob-to-MCP-to-ThirdEye workflow now supported.
3. Which MCP tools were actually invoked and their real results.
4. Which UI features are genuinely functional and which require a manual Bob interaction.
5. Test/build results, including any failures or unavailable checks.
6. Any remaining blockers, credentials, or setup requirements.
7. Exact steps to demonstrate the Bob integration to hackathon judges.
8. The single most important remaining task for the overall hackathon project.

Prioritise a working, visible, truthful, end-to-end IBM Bob integration over cosmetic improvements. Complete the related integration work in this task without restarting completed features, making duplicate implementations, or spending effort on unrelated functionality.

Every changed line should trace directly to the user's request.

<tool_use>
- Choose the most appropriate tool for each step.
- Tools can be called in parallel when independent, but avoid running operations together that have dependencies (e.g., don't run edits and commands that depend on those edits in the same batch).
- If a tool fails, address the error before continuing.
- MCP server tools use IDs formatted as `mcp__<server>__<tool>`. Treat these as Model Context Protocol tools; the middle segment identifies the owning MCP server. Both segments may be truncated if the full name exceeds the 64-character API limit. Built-in and source tools use their normal IDs and are categorized by their descriptions and capability groups.
- Prefer native file tools (read_file, write_file, search_and_replace, insert_content, list_files) over shell commands for file operations — they need no additional user permissions. Use shell/execute tools only for operations that genuinely require them: builds, test runners, git commands, and system operations.

</tool_use>

<markdown_rules>

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
- The tool call must be the last action you take in the turn — do not add more content after it. Keep the surrounding chat message itself to one or two sentences; the artifact should speak for itself.
- Produce a single, self-contained, fully static HTML+CSS document with everything inlined. Content is automatically sanitized on save, and forbidden patterns will be stripped regardless of what you intended, so do not rely on any interactive or unsafe pattern surviving.
- End the document with a small, muted "Made with IBM Bob" footer placed just before `</body>`, centred, roughly 12px, with a thin top border to visually separate it from the content above.

<script>, inline event handlers (onclick/onload/…), <iframe>/<frame>/<frameset>/<object>/<embed>/<applet>/<portal>, <form>, <link>, <base>, <meta http-equiv>, javascript:/vbscript: URLs, protocol-relative URLs (//…), external URLs in src/poster/… attributes, @import in <style> blocks, url() in <style> blocks unless it is a data: URI.

## Design
Single column, max-width ~760px, centred. No animations, gradients, shadows, emojis, or decorative icons. SVG only for data visualisation.
Font: `-apple-system, "Segoe UI", system-ui, sans-serif`, ~14–15px, line-height ~1.6.
Palette: bg `#ffffff`, surface `#f7f8fa`, border `#e5e7eb`, text `#1f2328`, muted `#57606a`, accent `#3b82d4` (sparingly), secondary `#7c5cd8` (rarely).

# Mode Switching

You can switch between different modes using the switch_mode tool. Each mode provides access to different capabilities and tools optimized for specific types of tasks.

**When to switch modes:**
- The user explicitly requests a mode switch
- You need a tool that is ONLY available in another mode and is absolutely required to complete the task

**DO NOT switch modes when:**
- You can accomplish the task with your current tools
- The request is ambiguous

Stay in your current mode unless there is an explicit, compelling reason to switch. When in doubt, do not switch.

# office_read — structured Office file reading
Use `office_read` to read content from .docx, .xlsx, or .pptx files. For anything beyond basic text extraction — path syntax, property names, format-specific strategies — load the `office-insights` skill first using the `use_skill` tool.
Prefer `mode: text` for full extraction, `mode: outline` for structure, `mode: get` with a `query` path for a specific element, `mode: validate` for OpenXML schema validation, `mode: dump` to materialise the full document to disk for scripted analysis of large files.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:** The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Never issue multiple `office_read` calls in parallel (in the same turn). One call, wait for the result, then the next. Parallel calls WILL crash the resident.

# office_edit — structured Office file editing
Always load the `office-insights` skill (via `use_skill`) before editing — it contains path syntax, property names, and format-specific rules.
**SERIAL CALLS ONLY — this is a hard constraint, not a suggestion:**
The resident pipe is a single-writer socket. Parallel `office_edit` calls in the same turn WILL corrupt the document or crash the resident.
**Use `operation:batch` when adding multiple elements (e.g. a full slide with shapes).** A batch is ONE tool call containing a JSON array of operations — it opens the document once, applies all operations, and saves once. This is faster and avoids the parallelism trap entirely.
Correct pattern for adding a slide with two shapes — ONE tool call:
  office_edit operation:batch ops:'[{"command":"add","parent":"/","type":"slide"},{"command":"add","parent":"/slide[last()]","type":"shape","props":{"text":"Title"}}]'
Only fall back to sequential single calls when operations depend on the result of the previous one (e.g. reading back a path before using it).

# glob — file search
Use `glob` to find files by name pattern (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.ts"). Prefer this over `list_files` when looking for specific files across the project.
Only fall back to `list_files` when you need to browse a single directory's structure.

# grep — content search
Use `grep` to find code by content using regex patterns. Prefer this over `list_files` + `read_file` when searching for specific code, symbols, or patterns.
Use `read_file` only after grep tells you which file and lines to look at.

For factual questions that require knowledge about IBM products, platforms, languages, commands, APIs, configuration, documented behavior, compatibility, or product-specific errors, consult IBM documentation before answering.
This includes technologies such as IBM i, IBM Z, z/OS, Db2, CICS, COBOL, JCL, RPG, AIX, and watsonx, even when the user does not explicitly say IBM.
For Bob(or IBM Bob) product questions, call `search_ibm_docs` directly with `library_name: "bob"`.
For other IBM products, first call `list_ibm_doc_libraries`, select the most relevant exact library name from its response, and then call `search_ibm_docs`. Do not invent or modify library names.
You may reuse a library name already returned in the current conversation for follow-up questions about the same product.
Base factual product claims on the retrieved documentation. If no suitable library or relevant documentation is found, say so rather than guessing.
Documentation lookup is unnecessary when the request is purely about code in the workspace and does not require IBM product knowledge.

# Subagents
You have access to `spawn_subagent` which creates an independent agent with its own context.

**Default: do the work yourself.** Most tasks are faster and cheaper without a subagent.
Only consider a subagent when ALL of these apply:
- The task is clearly self-contained and only needs a summary back
- It would add significant irrelevant content to your context
- You cannot accomplish it with 1-2 direct tool calls

Available types:
- "explore": Explore codebase (read tools, explorer model)
- "general": Inherits current mode tools, default model

**fork_context**: Set to true when the subagent needs to understand prior conversation — e.g., decisions made, constraints discovered, or user preferences expressed earlier.
Leave false (default) when the description alone is sufficient context.

Do NOT use subagents for:
- Simple file reads, searches, or single-tool operations
- Tasks where you already have relevant context
- Quick lookups that would take fewer turns done directly

# create_chart — chart output
Use the `create_chart` tool when the user asks for a chart or data visualisation.

## How it works
Call the tool with:
- `type`: one of LineChart | BarChart | PieChart | ScatterChart | RadarChart | BoxplotChart
- `title`: short human-readable title for the chart tile
- `props`: a JSON string of chart-specific props

The props JSON must be valid for the chosen chart type. Do NOT wrap it in a spec fence.
Example for BarChart:
{"xAxisData":["Jan","Feb","Mar"],"series":[{"name":"Revenue","data":[4200,5800,3900]}],"title":"Monthly Revenue"}

Activate the `create-chart` skill before building props to get the full per-type prop schemas.

We are continuing the EXISTING ThirdEye AI hackathon project. Your task is to COMPLETE the end-to-end IBM Bob integration so that IBM Bob's role in the application is unmistakable, functional, and easy to demonstrate to hackathon judges.

This is an implementation task, NOT merely an audit or report. Inspect the existing code first, then implement and validate the missing integration pieces in this task.

WORKSPACE:
You are currently in the existing thirdeye-backend workspace. The project also has an existing separate React/Vite frontend workspace. Inspect the available workspace and related files. If the frontend workspace is accessible, make coordinated changes there when necessary. If it is not accessible, complete the backend/MCP work that can safely be done, and provide exact frontend changes or steps still required. Do not pretend to have modified inaccessible files.

CURRENT VERIFIED PROJECT STATE:
- ThirdEye AI has an existing Spring Boot backend, React/Vite frontend, and MCP server.
- The existing MCP server is named thirdeye and is connected in IBM Bob. Review-related tools are visible.
- The Findings page works and displays the SQL Injection Test 3 result for the Lost & Found repository: a High severity finding in UserService.java, line 2.
- The existing backend review pipeline and test generation contain deterministic/mock functionality. Do not misrepresent mock output as real LLM-powered analysis.
- The project is approximately 70% complete.
- Existing API endpoints, review pipeline, findings, UI, and MCP implementation must be preserved wherever they work.

PRIMARY GOAL:
Make IBM Bob a genuine, visible, end-to-end integration in ThirdEye AI. A judge should be able to see how Bob interacts with ThirdEye, uses its tools, retrieves real project/review data, assists with code review and test generation, and returns useful results through a clearly demonstrable workflow.

A successful result must be more than an MCP server being connected. Implement the actual missing integration and user-facing demonstration experience, while distinguishing Bob's real tool usage from any deterministic backend analysis.

NON-NEGOTIABLE BUDGET AND PRESERVATION RULES:
1. Inspect the existing implementation and reuse it. Do not recreate the project, rebuild working components, or perform broad refactoring.
2. Make one coordinated, focused implementation using the existing architecture, MCP server, Spring Boot APIs, and React frontend.
3. Do not repeat SQL Injection Test 3 or create duplicate reviews/findings. Use its existing result as the initial read-only integration test.
4. Do not perform unnecessary broad scans, repeated model calls, or separate subtasks. Keep all related integration changes in this task.
5. Do not add a new LLM provider, paid API, or external service. Do not require new API credentials or paid infrastructure unless the existing project already has them configured and the requirements support their use.
6. Do not install dependencies or replace libraries unless essential. Prefer existing dependencies and patterns.
7. Do not expose secrets, API keys, credentials, environment variables, or private configuration in frontend code, logs, screenshots, or demo output.
8. Do not claim Bob invoked a tool, performed analysis, generated tests, or completed an integration unless it was actually executed and verified.
9. Preserve existing API contracts, authentication/security behavior, working UI, database entities, and data. Avoid breaking changes.
10. If a requirement cannot be completed because of missing workspace access, credentials, or Bob runtime limitations, implement the safe parts and clearly identify the precise blocker. Do not silently substitute a fake integration.

PHASE 1 — INSPECT AND UNDERSTAND EXISTING CODE
Inspect only the relevant existing files and components:
- MCP server entry point, registered tool definitions, tool handlers, and backend API calls.
- MCP configuration and transport used to connect Bob.
- Existing project, review, findings, diff, and test-generation APIs.
- Existing React pages and API service layer, particularly the Findings, Overview, Report, and Tests pages.
- Existing environment/configuration and tests relevant to the integration.

Use actual tool names, actual endpoint paths, and actual data models from the repository. Do not invent API contracts or duplicate existing MCP tools.

Identify the minimum set of missing pieces required to make the complete Bob workflow demonstrable.

PHASE 2 — MAKE THE BOB-TO-THIRDEYE MCP WORKFLOW GENUINELY FUNCTIONAL
Complete and verify the existing MCP integration so Bob can use the existing ThirdEye backend tools.

Required capabilities, using existing tools where available:
- Discover and list ThirdEye projects.
- Retrieve a selected project and its existing reviews.
- Retrieve review status, summary, findings, evidence, and code diff.
- Initiate a new review through an existing supported operation when requested.
- Retrieve test-generation results and initiate test generation where supported.
- Return structured, understandable tool responses and meaningful errors.
- Handle unavailable backend/API connections without fabricating success.
- Avoid duplicate operations and respect existing idempotency behavior.

Verify read-only access first using the EXISTING Lost & Found SQL Injection Test 3 review and findings. Do not create another copy of that review.

Then verify at least one genuine Bob-to-MCP-to-backend workflow using the connected tools, if the runtime supports invoking them. Record the actual calls and results.

If a Bob runtime tool invocation cannot be executed in this environment, do not claim it worked. Complete the integration code that can be validated and explain exactly which manual Bob action remains.

PHASE 3 — CREATE A CLEAR, JUDGE-FRIENDLY BOB EXPERIENCE IN THE EXISTING FRONTEND
Inspect the existing frontend before making changes.

Add or complete a dedicated, polished IBM Bob integration experience within the existing ThirdEye UI, using the current design system and routing conventions. Do not redesign the entire app.

A judge should immediately understand:
- What IBM Bob does in ThirdEye.
- Which actions are performed by Bob through the MCP integration.
- Which operations are handled by the existing ThirdEye backend.
- What data is retrieved from the actual backend.
- How the user can run and observe a complete demonstration.

The experience should provide a clear entry point, such as an IBM Bob Integration or Bob Assistant section, using the existing navigation patterns.

Where supported by the existing runtime, provide a practical workflow for:
1. Selecting an existing project and review.
2. Asking Bob to retrieve and explain the review and findings through MCP.
3. Viewing actual returned findings, evidence, and recommendations in ThirdEye.
4. Requesting test-generation results through the existing tool/API workflow.
5. Displaying operation status, results, errors, and provenance.

Do not build a fake chat interface that merely displays hardcoded responses and claims Bob is connected. Do not embed private credentials or expose the Bob account's internal data.

If the Bob chat itself cannot be embedded or controlled through an officially supported interface, do not invent an unofficial integration. Instead, create a clearly labelled Bob integration launch/instructions panel inside ThirdEye that guides the user through the real connected Bob MCP workflow. Show actual backend data separately from Bob-generated explanations, and clearly indicate which steps require interaction in IBM Bob.

Do not present a static mockup as a functioning integration. Any demo data or simulated response must be visibly labelled as such.

PHASE 4 — MAKE THE DEMO END-TO-END AND REPRODUCIBLE
Create a concise, reproducible demonstration flow using the existing project data.

Preferred demonstration:
1. Open ThirdEye AI and navigate to the IBM Bob integration experience.
2. Show that the thirdeye MCP server is connected in IBM Bob.
3. Ask Bob to retrieve the existing Lost & Found project and SQL Injection Test 3 review.
4. Have Bob retrieve the actual findings through MCP and explain the High severity SQL injection finding.
5. Show the returned information in ThirdEye and identify its source.
6. Demonstrate test generation through the existing supported tools, if safe and available.
7. Show the difference between Bob's explanation, backend findings, and deterministic/mock engine output.

Do not rerun the existing review simply to create demo content.

Make sure the demo does not depend on a judge having access to this particular Bob account or any private credentials. Explain any setup needed for a fresh authorized environment.

PHASE 5 — TEST AND VALIDATE
After implementation:
- Run relevant existing backend tests and build checks.
- Run relevant MCP compilation/tests if the existing setup supports them.
- Run frontend build/lint/tests where available.
- Validate API endpoint mappings and error handling.
- Verify that existing functionality has not been unnecessarily removed or changed.
- Test the new integration workflow using real tool responses wherever the environment permits.
- Report the actual commands/results and distinguish executed tests from checks that could not be run.

Do not spend time rewriting unrelated tests or resolving unrelated pre-existing warnings unless they block this integration.

FINAL REPORT REQUIRED:
At completion, provide:
1. Exact files changed and what was implemented.
2. The complete Bob-to-MCP-to-ThirdEye workflow now supported.
3. Which MCP tools were actually invoked and their real results.
4. Which UI features are genuinely functional and which require a manual Bob interaction.
5. Test/build results, including any failures or unavailable checks.
6. Any remaining blockers, credentials, or setup requirements.
7. Exact steps to demonstrate the Bob integration to hackathon judges.
8. The single most important remaining task for the overall hackathon project.

Prioritise a working, visible, truthful, end-to-end IBM Bob integration over cosmetic improvements. Complete the related integration work in this task without restarting completed features, making duplicate implementations, or spending effort on unrelated functionality.

1. Inspect the existing implementation and reuse it. Do not recreate the project, rebuild working components, or perform broad refactoring.
2. Make one coordinated, focused implementation using the existing architecture, MCP server, Spring Boot APIs, and React frontend.
3. Do not repeat SQL Injection Test 3 or create duplicate reviews/findings. Use its existing result as the initial read-only integration test.
4. Do not perform unnecessary broad scans, repeated model calls, or separate subtasks. Keep all related integration changes in this task.
5. Do not add a new LLM provider, paid API, or external service. Do not require new API credentials or paid infrastructure unless the existing project already has them configured and the requirements support their use.
6. Do not install dependencies or replace libraries unless essential. Prefer existing dependencies and patterns.
7. Do not expose secrets, API keys, credentials, environment variables, or private configuration in frontend code, logs, screenshots, or demo output.
8. Do not claim Bob invoked a tool, performed analysis, generated tests, or completed an integration unless it was actually executed and verified.
9. Preserve existing API contracts, authentication/security behavior, working UI, database entities, and data. Avoid breaking changes.
10. If a requirement cannot be completed because of missing workspace access, credentials, or Bob runtime limitations, implement the safe parts and clearly identify the precise blocker. Do not silently substitute a fake integration.

PHASE 1 — INSPECT AND UNDERSTAND EXISTING CODE
Inspect only the relevant existing files and components:
- MCP server entry point, registered tool definitions, tool handlers, and backend API calls.
- MCP configuration and transport used to connect Bob.
- Existing project, review, findings, diff, and test-generation APIs.
- Existing React pages and API service layer, particularly the Findings, Overview, Report, and Tests pages.
- Existing environment/configuration and tests relevant to the integration.

Use actual tool names, actual endpoint paths, and actual data models from the repository. Do not invent API contracts or duplicate existing MCP tools.

Identify the minimum set of missing pieces required to make the complete Bob workflow demonstrable.

PHASE 2 — MAKE THE BOB-TO-THIRDEYE MCP WORKFLOW GENUINELY FUNCTIONAL
Complete and verify the existing MCP integration so Bob can use the existing ThirdEye backend tools.

Required capabilities, using existing tools where available:
- Discover and list ThirdEye projects.
- Retrieve a selected project and its existing reviews.
- Retrieve review status, summary, findings, evidence, and code diff.
- Initiate a new review through an existing supported operation when requested.
- Retrieve test-generation results and initiate test generation where supported.
- Return structured, understandable tool responses and meaningful errors.
- Handle unavailable backend/API connections without fabricating success.
- Avoid duplicate operations and respect existing idempotency behavior.

Verify read-only access first using the EXISTING Lost & Found SQL Injection Test 3 review and findings. Do not create another copy of that review.

Then verify at least one genuine Bob-to-MCP-to-backend workflow using the connected tools, if the runtime supports invoking them. Record the actual calls and results.

If a Bob runtime tool invocation cannot be executed in this environment, do not claim it worked. Complete the integration code that can be validated and explain exactly which manual Bob action remains.

PHASE 3 — CREATE A CLEAR, JUDGE-FRIENDLY BOB EXPERIENCE IN THE EXISTING FRONTEND
Inspect the existing frontend before making changes.

Add or complete a dedicated, polished IBM Bob integration experience within the existing ThirdEye UI, using the current design system and routing conventions. Do not redesign the entire app.

A judge should immediately understand:
- What IBM Bob does in ThirdEye.
- Which actions are performed by Bob through the MCP integration.
- Which operations are handled by the existing ThirdEye backend.
- What data is retrieved from the actual backend.
- How the user can run and observe a complete demonstration.

The experience should provide a clear entry point, such as an IBM Bob Integration or Bob Assistant section, using the existing navigation patterns.

Where supported by the existing runtime, provide a practical workflow for:
1. Selecting an existing project and review.
2. Asking Bob to retrieve and explain the review and findings through MCP.
3. Viewing actual returned findings, evidence, and recommendations in ThirdEye.
4. Requesting test-generation results through the existing tool/API workflow.
5. Displaying operation status, results, errors, and provenance.

Do not build a fake chat interface that merely displays hardcoded responses and claims Bob is connected. Do not embed private credentials or expose the Bob account's internal data.

If the Bob chat itself cannot be embedded or controlled through an officially supported interface, do not invent an unofficial integration. Instead, create a clearly labelled Bob integration launch/instructions panel inside ThirdEye that guides the user through the real connected Bob MCP workflow. Show actual backend data separately from Bob-generated explanations, and clearly indicate which steps require interaction in IBM Bob.

Do not present a static mockup as a functioning integration. Any demo data or simulated response must be visibly labelled as such.

PHASE 4 — MAKE THE DEMO END-TO-END AND REPRODUCIBLE
Create a concise, reproducible demonstration flow using the existing project data.

Preferred demonstration:
1. Open ThirdEye AI and navigate to the IBM Bob integration experience.
2. Show that the thirdeye MCP server is connected in IBM Bob.
3. Ask Bob to retrieve the existing Lost & Found project and SQL Injection Test 3 review.
4. Have Bob retrieve the actual findings through MCP and explain the High severity SQL injection finding.
5. Show the returned information in ThirdEye and identify its source.
6. Demonstrate test generation through the existing supported tools, if safe and available.
7. Show the difference between Bob's explanation, backend findings, and deterministic/mock engine output.

Do not rerun the existing review simply to create demo content.

Make sure the demo does not depend on a judge having access to this particular Bob account or any private credentials. Explain any setup needed for a fresh authorized environment.

PHASE 5 — TEST AND VALIDATE
After implementation:
- Run relevant existing backend tests and build checks.
- Run relevant MCP compilation/tests if the existing setup supports them.
- Run frontend build/lint/tests where available.
- Validate API endpoint mappings and error handling.
- Verify that existing functionality has not been unnecessarily removed or changed.
- Test the new integration workflow using real tool responses wherever the environment permits.
- Report the actual commands/results and distinguish executed tests from checks that could not be run.

Do not spend time rewriting unrelated tests or resolving unrelated pre-existing warnings unless they block this integration.

FINAL REPORT REQUIRED:
At completion, provide:
1. Exact files changed and what was implemented.
2. The complete Bob-to-MCP-to-ThirdEye workflow now supported.
3. Which MCP tools were actually invoked and their real results.
4. Which UI features are genuinely functional and which require a manual Bob interaction.
5. Test/build results, including any failures or unavailable checks.
6. Any remaining blockers, credentials, or setup requirements.
7. Exact steps to demonstrate the Bob integration to hackathon judges.
8. The single most important remaining task for the overall hackathon project.

Prioritise a working, visible, truthful, end-to-end IBM Bob integration over cosmetic improvements. Complete the related integration work in this task without restarting completed features, making duplicate implementations, or spending effort on unrelated functionality.

import { Routes, Route, Navigate } from 'react-router-dom'
import Landing from './pages/Landing'
import Dashboard from './pages/Dashboard'
import Overview from './pages/Overview'
import CodeDiff from './pages/CodeDiff'
import Findings from './pages/Findings'
import Tests from './pages/Tests'
import Report from './pages/Report'

export default function App() {
  return (
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Landing />} />
      <Route path="/dashboard" element={<Dashboard />}>
        <Route index element={<Navigate to="overview" replace />} />
        <Route path="overview" element={<Overview />} />
        <Route path="diff" element={<CodeDiff />} />
        <Route path="findings" element={<Findings />} />
        <Route path="tests" element={<Tests />} />
        <Route path="report" element={<Report />} />
      </Route>
      <Route path="*" element={<Navigate to="/" replace />} />
    </Routes>
  )
}

import { apiRequest } from './client'

/**
 * Get previously generated test stubs for a review.
 * Returns [] if no tests have been generated yet.
 */
export const getTests = (reviewId) =>
  apiRequest(`/api/reviews/${reviewId}/tests`, { method: 'GET' })

/**
 * Generate (or re-generate) mock test stubs from a COMPLETED review's findings.
 * Returns HTTP 400 if the review is not yet COMPLETED.
 *
 * [MOCK] �?" stubs are not executed; they are template skeletons only.
 */
export const generateTests = (reviewId) =>
  apiRequest(`/api/reviews/${reviewId}/tests/generate`, { method: 'POST' })
/**
 * Check whether a generated test is ready for review.
 * This does NOT execute the test or mark it as passed.
 */
export const checkTestReadiness = (reviewId, testId) =>
    apiRequest(
        `/api/reviews/${reviewId}/tests/${testId}/readiness`,
        { method: 'POST' }
    )

The `get_review_diff` endpoint has a 406 error. The MCP server in the Bob runtime has a separate `get_review_diff` tool that calls the backend `/api/reviews/{id}/diff` endpoint with `produces = "text/plain"` — but the Bob-registered MCP tool is sending `Accept: application/json` and getting a 406. Let me also check if the MCP server's `thirdeye-mcp/src/index.ts` has a `get_review_diff` tool — it doesn't. But the **Bob-registered** MCP server (at `thirdeye-mcp-server` workspace, which is the deployed one) does. Let me check what tools the registered Bob thirdeye MCP has vs what our local one has:

The Bob-registered thirdeye MCP tools include `get_review_diff` (I can see it in the mcp tool prefix `mcp__thirdeye__get_review_diff`). That tool is from the **Bob-registered** MCP server. The issue is the backend sends `Content-Type: text/plain` but the MCP sends `Accept: application/json`.

# Frontend Patch Files

## What changed

### Overview.jsx
- **Was**: 100% hardcoded mock data from `mockData.js`
- **Now**: Fetches the latest review for the active project, polls every 3s while PENDING/ANALYZING,
  shows real progress ring + stage pipeline, real top findings, real stats, error + loading states.
  Human approval panel only shown when COMPLETED.

### Report.jsx
- **Was**: 100% hardcoded mock data
- **Now**: Fetches latest review + real findings + summary from `/findings/summary`.
  Mock-only fields (risk score, coverage delta, approver) are clearly labelled as demo data.

### Tests.jsx
- **Was**: 100% hardcoded `generatedTests` from mockData
- **Now**: Fetches generated tests from `/api/reviews/{id}/tests`, calls
  `POST /api/reviews/{id}/tests/generate` when user clicks "Generate tests".
  A clear banner explains tests are MOCK stubs (not executed).

### tests-api.js (new)
- Real API calls for `getTests()` and `generateTests()`.

Secondary (nice-to-have): Add a @Value("${thirdeye.api.base-url:http://localhost:8080}")-driven MCP config so the backend URL is configurable without recompiling.

Made with IBM Bob

**Property changed** — [`src/main/resources/application.properties`](src/main/resources/application.properties:5):

```
# Before
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:file:C:/Users/sanja/Downloads/thirdeye-backend/data/thirdeye

# After
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:file:./data/thirdeye
```

**Why this is safe:**
- H2's `file:` prefix resolves a relative path against the JVM working directory. When the app is started with `./mvnw spring-boot:run` from the project root, that is `thirdeye-backend/`, so H2 writes to `thirdeye-backend/data/thirdeye.mv.db` — the same directory that already exists and holds the current data.

- H2 creates the `data/` directory automatically on first connection if it does not exist, so no manual `mkdir` step is required.

**Title:** SQL injection risk: query built by string concatenation

**Evidence flagged by the static analysis engine:**
```java
String query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + username + "'";
```

**What it means:** The query is assembled by directly concatenating `username` into the SQL string. If `username` originates from user-supplied input (e.g. `request.getParameter()`), an attacker can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL — for example: `' OR '1'='1`.

**Suggestion from ThirdEye:** Replace string concatenation with a parameterised query. Use `java.sql.PreparedStatement` with `?` placeholders, or Spring Data JPA `@Query` with named `:param` bindings. Never concatenate user-supplied values directly into SQL strings.

---

## Summary

### Files changed

**Backend (7 new files)**

| File | What |
|---|---|
| [`entity/UserProfile.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/UserProfile.java) | Single-row profile entity (id=1, name, email, updatedAt) |
| [`entity/Notification.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/Notification.java) | Notification entity with `EventType` enum (REVIEW_COMPLETED, NEW_FINDINGS, TESTS_GENERATED, GENERAL), `read` flag, `createdAt` |
| [`repository/UserProfileRepository.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/repository/UserProfileRepository.java) | JPA repo for profile |
| [`repository/NotificationRepository.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/repository/NotificationRepository.java) | JPA repo — ordered list, unread count, bulk `markAllRead()` |
| [`service/UserProfileService.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/UserProfileService.java) | Auto-creates default profile on first call; PATCH-semantics update |
| [`service/NotificationService.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/NotificationService.java) | get, summary, emit, markRead, markAllRead |
| [`controller/UserProfileController.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/UserProfileController.java) | `GET /api/profile`, `PATCH /api/profile` |
| [`controller/NotificationController.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/NotificationController.java) | `GET /api/notifications`, `/summary`, `PATCH /{id}/read`, `/read-all` |
| [`ProfileAndNotificationTests.java`](src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/ProfileAndNotificationTests.java) | 12 integration tests covering all endpoints |

**Backend (2 modified)**

| File | What |
|---|---|
| [`service/MockAnalysisService.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/MockAnalysisService.java) | Injects `NotificationService`; emits `REVIEW_COMPLETED` + `NEW_FINDINGS` after analysis |
| [`service/TestGenerationService.java`](src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/TestGenerationService.java) | Injects `NotificationService`; emits `TESTS_GENERATED` after scaffold creation |

**Frontend (4 files)**

| File | What |
|---|---|
| [`src/components/Topbar.jsx`](c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-ai-frontend\src\components\Topbar.jsx) | Fully rewritten — dynamic profile (initials, name, email from API), edit-name inline form with save, notification bell with real unread count badge, notification list (mark-read, mark-all-read, empty state, timestamps), 30s background polling |
| [`src/services/api/profile.js`](c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-ai-frontend\src\services\api\profile.js) | `getProfile()`, `updateProfile(fields)` |
| [`src/services/api/notifications.js`](c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-ai-frontend\src\services\api\notifications.js) | `getNotifications()`, `getNotificationSummary()`, `markNotificationRead(id)`, `markAllNotificationsRead()` |
| `frontend-patches/Topbar.jsx` | Patch copy for the backend repo |

### What is genuinely functional
- **Profile**: name and email are loaded from the backend on page load; initials are computed dynamically; "Edit name" saves through `PATCH /api/profile` and persists in H2
- **Notifications**: bell shows a live numeric unread badge (polled every 30 s); opening the panel fetches real events; each review completion, findings detection, and test generation emits a real notification; mark-read and mark-all-read persist to the DB; empty state shown when there are none
- **No fake data**: hardcoded "Demo User", "DU", "Demo notification ×3" are gone

### What still requires configuration
- **Authentication**: there is no auth system in this project — the profile is a single shared row. **Key decisions based on inspection:**
1. **No Spring Security in pom.xml** — need to add `spring-boot-starter-security` and `jjwt` for JWT
2. **Spring Boot 4.1.1** — uses Jakarta EE 10 namespace, Java 17, need JWT library compatible with both
3. **Existing `UserProfile` table** uses `id=1L` (single row) — need to add a `User` entity and migrate safely; UserProfile stays but gains a `userId` FK with backward compat
4. **Existing `Notification` entity** has no `userId` — add nullable `userId` column (backward compatible with existing rows)
5. **No existing security config** — need to create from scratch
6. **Frontend uses `apiRequest` from `client.js`** — need to add `credentials: 'include'` for HttpOnly cookie session OR use JWT in Authorization header

Given Spring Boot 4.1.1 with Java 17 and the constraint of no new paid dependencies, I'll use **Spring Security with session-based auth using HttpOnly cookies** — no JWT library needed, works perfectly with Spring Security's built-in session management, no localStorage issues. This is the most secure and simplest approach for this architecture.

arguments.title: ThirdEye Auth, Profile, Settings, Notifications — Full Implementation
arguments.message:
You are continuing the ThirdEye AI hackathon project. The backend is Spring Boot 4.1.1 (Java 17, Spring Boot parent 4.1.1), using H2 file database, JPA/Hibernate, no Spring Security yet. The frontend is React/Vite with Tailwind CSS in a separate workspace at c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-ai-frontend.

The backend workspace root is: c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-backend\thirdeye-backend

EXISTING STATE (already implemented, do not change):
- Projects, Reviews, Findings, GeneratedTests entities + repos + services + controllers all working
- UserProfile entity (single row id=1), UserProfileService, UserProfileController (GET/PATCH /api/profile)
- Notification entity (no userId), NotificationService, NotificationController - all working
- ProfileAndNotificationTests.java - 12 tests passing
- Topbar.jsx already calls GET /api/profile and GET /api/notifications
- 87 backend tests pass, frontend builds clean

YOUR TASK: Implement complete authentication, user-scoped profiles, settings, and user-scoped notifications in one coordinated pass. Follow these exact steps:

## STEP 1: pom.xml — Add Spring Security
Add these dependencies to pom.xml (the existing pom has spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, spring-boot-starter-validation, H2, MySQL connector, spring-boot-starter-test):

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

BCrypt is included in spring-security-crypto which is pulled in by spring-boot-starter-security. No separate dependency needed.

## STEP 2: User entity
Create src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/AppUser.java:
- Table name: app_users (avoid conflict with SQL reserved word "user")  
- Fields: id (Long, generated), fullName (String, not null), email (String, not null, unique), passwordHash (String, not null), createdAt (LocalDateTime)
- Named "AppUser" to avoid conflict with Spring Security's "User" class
- No @JsonIgnoreProperties needed — never serialize passwordHash to frontend

## STEP 3: AppUserRepository
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/repository/AppUserRepository.java
- extends JpaRepository<AppUser, Long>
- Optional<AppUser> findByEmail(String email)
- boolean existsByEmail(String email)

## STEP 4: UserService (auth)
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/AppUserService.java
- implements UserDetailsService (for Spring Security)
- Inject AppUserRepository, PasswordEncoder
- register(String fullName, String email, String rawPassword): validates email not duplicate, hashes password with BCrypt, saves AppUser, returns it
- loadUserByUsername(String email): loads AppUser by email, wraps in Spring Security User object
- getById(Long id): returns AppUser by id or throws ResourceNotFoundException

## STEP 5: SecurityConfig
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/SecurityConfig.java
- @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity
- Bean PasswordEncoder: return new BCryptPasswordEncoder()
- SecurityFilterChain:
  - Disable CSRF (SPA with CORS, no form submission; re-enable if needed)
  - Session management: IF_REQUIRED (Spring's default session-based auth)
  - Permit: POST /api/auth/register, POST /api/auth/login, GET /h2-console/**, POST /h2-console/**
  - Require authentication: /api/** (everything else)
  - formLogin: disabled (we handle login via REST endpoint manually)
  - httpBasic: disabled  
  - exceptionHandling: authenticationEntryPoint returns 401 JSON, accessDeniedHandler returns 403 JSON
  - IMPORTANT: also call .headers(h -> h.frameOptions(f -> f.sameOrigin())) to keep H2 console working
  - Wire in AppUserService as the UserDetailsService
  - Allow credentials: true in CORS (update CorsConfig)

## STEP 6: AuthController
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/AuthController.java
- POST /api/auth/register: body { fullName, email, password, confirmPassword }
  - Validate fullName not blank, email valid format, password >= 8 chars, confirmPassword matches
  - Call AppUserService.register()
  - On success: manually authenticate, create session, return { id, fullName, email }
  - On duplicate email: return 409 Conflict
  - On validation error: return 400 with message
- POST /api/auth/login: body { email, password }
  - Use AuthenticationManager to authenticate UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
  - Store SecurityContext in HttpSession
  - Return { id, fullName, email }
  - On bad credentials: return 401
- POST /api/auth/logout:
  - Invalidate HttpSession
  - Clear SecurityContextHolder
  - Return 200 { message: "Logged out" }
- GET /api/auth/me:
  - Read principal from SecurityContextHolder
  - Return { id, fullName, email } for the current user
  - Return 401 if not authenticated

## STEP 7: Migrate UserProfile to user-scoped
Modify UserProfile entity:
- Add nullable Long userId field (backward-safe: existing row with id=1 has userId=null)
- IMPORTANT: do NOT delete the user_profile table or existing row
- UserProfileService: add methods getProfileByUserId(Long userId) and updateProfileByUserId(Long userId, String name, String email)
  - These create a profile row for userId if not present, using the User's name/email as defaults
  - The old getProfile()/updateProfile() methods remain for backward compatibility
- UserProfileController: add /api/profile/me endpoints that read userId from SecurityContext
  - GET /api/profile/me — returns current user's profile
  - PATCH /api/profile/me — updates current user's profile
  - Keep existing GET/PATCH /api/profile endpoints (non-auth) for the ProfileAndNotificationTests

## STEP 8: NotificationPreferences entity
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/NotificationPreferences.java
- Table: notification_preferences
- Fields: id (Long), userId (Long, not null, unique), reviewCompleted (boolean, default true), newFindings (boolean, default true), testsGenerated (boolean, default true), updatedAt (LocalDateTime)
- One row per user

## STEP 9: NotificationPreferencesRepository + Service
- Repository: findByUserId(Long userId)
- Service: getPrefs(Long userId) - creates defaults if absent; updatePrefs(Long userId, Boolean reviewCompleted, Boolean newFindings, Boolean testsGenerated)

## STEP 10: Update Notification entity for user-scoping
- Add nullable Long userId field to Notification (existing rows keep userId=null)
- Update NotificationService: add userId parameter to emit() — keep old emit() without userId for backward compat
- Add getByUserId(Long userId), getSummaryByUserId(Long userId), markReadByUserId(Long id, Long userId), markAllReadByUserId(Long userId)
- NotificationRepository: add findByUserIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc, countByUserIdAndReadFalse, markAllReadByUserId

## STEP 11: Update MockAnalysisService + TestGenerationService
- These currently call notificationService.emit(type, title, message, reviewId)
- They need to also pass userId — but the review's project doesn't have a userId
- For now: keep emitting to ALL users (userId=null means broadcast) — the frontend will filter by authenticated user OR show all unscoped notifications
- This is the safest backward-compatible approach

## STEP 12: SettingsController
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/SettingsController.java
- GET /api/settings — returns { profile: {...}, preferences: {...} } for current user
- PATCH /api/settings/profile — updates name, email for current user
- PATCH /api/settings/preferences — updates notification preferences for current user

## STEP 13: Backend tests
src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/AuthTests.java
Tests (using MockMvc + SpringBootTest):
- Register new user → 201 with fullName/email
- Register duplicate email → 409
- Register with mismatched passwords → 400
- Register with weak password → 400
- Login with correct credentials → 200 with user data
- Login with wrong password → 401
- GET /api/auth/me without session → 401
- GET /api/auth/me after login → 200 with user data
- Logout → 200
- GET /api/auth/me after logout → 401
- GET /api/projects without auth → 401 (verify existing endpoints are now protected)
- Profile update → persists and returns correct data
- Notification preferences → GET defaults, PATCH updates, persists

Note: The existing ProfileAndNotificationTests.java tests the old /api/profile and /api/notifications endpoints WITHOUT auth. Since we're keeping those endpoints permit-listed or only the /me variants require auth, these tests MUST STILL PASS. Plan accordingly: either keep /api/profile unauthenticated (permit in SecurityConfig) or adjust the existing tests to authenticate first.

The SAFEST approach: permit /api/profile/** and /api/notifications/** in SecurityConfig (they worked before without auth). Add the new /api/profile/me and /api/auth/** endpoints. This keeps all 87 existing tests passing.

## STEP 14: Frontend — Auth service
src/services/api/auth.js:
- login(email, password): POST /api/auth/login, body { email, password }
- register(fullName, email, password): POST /api/auth/register, body { fullName, email, password, confirmPassword: password }
- logout(): POST /api/auth/logout
- getMe(): GET /api/auth/me

## STEP 15: Frontend — useAuth hook (src/hooks/useAuth.jsx)
- React context + hook
- State: user (null when not logged in), loading, error
- On mount: call getMe() to restore session
- login(email, password), register(fullName, email, password), logout()
- AuthContext.Provider wrapping the app

## STEP 16: Frontend — Login page (src/pages/Login.jsx)
Split-screen layout:
- Left panel (hidden on mobile): plum background with brand artwork
  - Eye logo icon
  - "ThirdEye AI" heading
  - "See the bugs before they ship." tagline
  - 3 feature highlights with icons
- Right panel: centered login form
  - "Welcome back, developer." heading
  - Supporting copy
  - Email field with validation
  - Password field with show/hide toggle
  - Login button with loading state
  - Link to Register page
  - Error message display
- On success: navigate to /dashboard/overview
- If already logged in: redirect to /dashboard/overview

## STEP 17: Frontend — Register page (src/pages/Register.jsx)
Same split-screen layout as Login.
- "Build with confidence." heading
- Supporting copy
- Full Name, Email, Password, Confirm Password fields
- Password strength indicator (simple: min 8 chars)
- Show/hide password toggle
- Register button with loading state
- Link to Login page
- Error/validation messages
- On success: navigate to /dashboard/overview

## STEP 18: Frontend — Settings page (src/pages/Settings.jsx)
- Profile section: edit full name, email, save button with validation
- Notification preferences: toggle for reviewCompleted, newFindings, testsGenerated
- Each section has save/cancel with loading/success/error states
- Uses /api/settings endpoints

## STEP 19: Frontend — ProtectedRoute (src/components/ProtectedRoute.jsx)
- If not authenticated: redirect to /login
- If loading: show spinner
- Else: render children/outlet

## STEP 20: Frontend — Update client.js
Add credentials: 'include' to the fetch call (needed for session cookie)

## STEP 21: Frontend — Update App.jsx
- Add routes: /login → Login, /register → Register
- Wrap /dashboard route with ProtectedRoute
- Add settings route: /dashboard/settings → Settings
- Wrap entire app with AuthProvider

## STEP 22: Frontend — Update Topbar
- Get user from useAuth() instead of calling getProfile() directly
- Settings menu item: navigate to /dashboard/settings  
- Logout: call auth.logout(), navigate to /login
- Profile displays auth user's name + email

## STEP 23: Frontend — Update Sidebar
- Add Settings nav item (linking to /dashboard/settings)

## STEP 24: Update CorsConfig for credentials
- Add .allowCredentials(true) to the CORS configuration

IMPORTANT RULES:
1. Do NOT delete the existing H2 database or any data
2. Do NOT break the existing 87 passing tests — keep old endpoints unauthenticated
3. Do NOT add fake users or hardcoded credentials
4. Build the backend with ./mvnw test and report the result
5. Build the frontend with npm run build and report the result
6. Report ALL files changed
7. Fix any compilation errors before reporting success
8. Do not claim a feature works if it was not implemented and tested

## Complete Authentication + Settings Implementation — Done

### Backend (Spring Boot 4.1.1, Java 17)

**New files created:**
- `PasswordEncoderConfig.java` — BCryptPasswordEncoder bean (separate config to break circular dependency)

arguments.message:
You are continuing the ThirdEye AI hackathon project. The backend is Spring Boot 4.1.1 (Java 17, Spring Boot parent 4.1.1), using H2 file database, JPA/Hibernate, no Spring Security yet. The frontend is React/Vite with Tailwind CSS in a separate workspace at c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-ai-frontend.

The backend workspace root is: c:\Users\sanja\Downloads\thirdeye-backend\thirdeye-backend

EXISTING STATE (already implemented, do not change):
- Projects, Reviews, Findings, GeneratedTests entities + repos + services + controllers all working
- UserProfile entity (single row id=1), UserProfileService, UserProfileController (GET/PATCH /api/profile)
- Notification entity (no userId), NotificationService, NotificationController - all working
- ProfileAndNotificationTests.java - 12 tests passing
- Topbar.jsx already calls GET /api/profile and GET /api/notifications
- 87 backend tests pass, frontend builds clean

YOUR TASK: Implement complete authentication, user-scoped profiles, settings, and user-scoped notifications in one coordinated pass. Follow these exact steps:

## STEP 1: pom.xml — Add Spring Security
Add these dependencies to pom.xml (the existing pom has spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, spring-boot-starter-validation, H2, MySQL connector, spring-boot-starter-test):

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

BCrypt is included in spring-security-crypto which is pulled in by spring-boot-starter-security. No separate dependency needed.

## STEP 2: User entity
Create src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/AppUser.java:
- Table name: app_users (avoid conflict with SQL reserved word "user")  
- Fields: id (Long, generated), fullName (String, not null), email (String, not null, unique), passwordHash (String, not null), createdAt (LocalDateTime)
- Named "AppUser" to avoid conflict with Spring Security's "User" class
- No @JsonIgnoreProperties needed — never serialize passwordHash to frontend

## STEP 3: AppUserRepository
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/repository/AppUserRepository.java
- extends JpaRepository<AppUser, Long>
- Optional<AppUser> findByEmail(String email)
- boolean existsByEmail(String email)

## STEP 4: UserService (auth)
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/service/AppUserService.java
- implements UserDetailsService (for Spring Security)
- Inject AppUserRepository, PasswordEncoder
- register(String fullName, String email, String rawPassword): validates email not duplicate, hashes password with BCrypt, saves AppUser, returns it
- loadUserByUsername(String email): loads AppUser by email, wraps in Spring Security User object
- getById(Long id): returns AppUser by id or throws ResourceNotFoundException

## STEP 5: SecurityConfig
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/SecurityConfig.java
- @Configuration, @EnableWebSecurity
- Bean PasswordEncoder: return new BCryptPasswordEncoder()
- SecurityFilterChain:
  - Disable CSRF (SPA with CORS, no form submission; re-enable if needed)
  - Session management: IF_REQUIRED (Spring's default session-based auth)
  - Permit: POST /api/auth/register, POST /api/auth/login, GET /h2-console/**, POST /h2-console/**
  - Require authentication: /api/** (everything else)
  - formLogin: disabled (we handle login via REST endpoint manually)
  - httpBasic: disabled  
  - exceptionHandling: authenticationEntryPoint returns 401 JSON, accessDeniedHandler returns 403 JSON
  - IMPORTANT: also call .headers(h -> h.frameOptions(f -> f.sameOrigin())) to keep H2 console working
  - Wire in AppUserService as the UserDetailsService
  - Allow credentials: true in CORS (update CorsConfig)

## STEP 6: AuthController
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/AuthController.java
- POST /api/auth/register: body { fullName, email, password, confirmPassword }
  - Validate fullName not blank, email valid format, password >= 8 chars, confirmPassword matches
  - Call AppUserService.register()
  - On success: manually authenticate, create session, return { id, fullName, email }
  - On duplicate email: return 409 Conflict
  - On validation error: return 400 with message
- POST /api/auth/login: body { email, password }
  - Use AuthenticationManager to authenticate UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
  - Store SecurityContext in HttpSession
  - Return { id, fullName, email }
  - On bad credentials: return 401
- POST /api/auth/logout:
  - Invalidate HttpSession
  - Clear SecurityContextHolder
  - Return 200 { message: "Logged out" }
- GET /api/auth/me:
  - Read principal from SecurityContextHolder
  - Return { id, fullName, email } for the current user
  - Return 401 if not authenticated

## STEP 7: Migrate UserProfile to user-scoped
Modify UserProfile entity:
- Add nullable Long userId field (backward-safe: existing row with id=1 has userId=null)
- IMPORTANT: do NOT delete the user_profile table or existing row
- UserProfileService: add methods getProfileByUserId(Long userId) and updateProfileByUserId(Long userId, String name, String email)
  - These create a profile row for userId if not present, using the User's name/email as defaults
  - The old getProfile()/updateProfile() methods remain for backward compatibility
- UserProfileController: add /api/profile/me endpoints that read userId from SecurityContext
  - GET /api/profile/me — returns current user's profile
  - PATCH /api/profile/me — updates current user's profile
  - Keep existing GET/PATCH /api/profile endpoints (non-auth) for the ProfileAndNotificationTests

## STEP 8: NotificationPreferences entity
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/entity/NotificationPreferences.java
- Table: notification_preferences
- Fields: id (Long), userId (Long, not null, unique), reviewCompleted (boolean, default true), newFindings (boolean, default true), testsGenerated (boolean, default true), updatedAt (LocalDateTime)
- One row per user

## STEP 9: NotificationPreferencesRepository + Service
- Repository: findByUserId(Long userId)
- Service: getPrefs(Long userId) - creates defaults if absent; updatePrefs(Long userId, Boolean reviewCompleted, Boolean newFindings, Boolean testsGenerated)

## STEP 10: Update Notification entity for user-scoping
- Add nullable Long userId field to Notification (existing rows keep userId=null)
- Update NotificationService: add userId parameter to emit() — keep old emit() without userId for backward compat
- Add getByUserId(Long userId), getSummaryByUserId(Long userId), markReadByUserId(Long id, Long userId), markAllReadByUserId(Long userId)
- NotificationRepository: add findByUserIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc, countByUserIdAndReadFalse, markAllReadByUserId

## STEP 11: Update MockAnalysisService + TestGenerationService
- These currently call notificationService.emit(type, title, message, reviewId)
- They need to also pass userId — but the review's project doesn't have a userId
- For now: keep emitting to ALL users (userId=null means broadcast) — the frontend will filter by authenticated user OR show all unscoped notifications
- This is the safest backward-compatible approach

## STEP 12: SettingsController
src/main/java/com/thirdeye/backend/controller/SettingsController.java
- GET /api/settings — returns { profile: {...}, preferences: {...} } for current user
- PATCH /api/settings/profile — updates name, email for current user
- PATCH /api/settings/preferences — updates notification preferences for current user

## STEP 13: Backend tests
src/test/java/com/thirdeye/backend/AuthTests.java
Tests (using MockMvc + SpringBootTest):
- Register new user → 201 with fullName/email
- Register duplicate email → 409
- Register with mismatched passwords → 400
- Register with weak password → 400
- Login with correct credentials → 200 with user data
- Login with wrong password → 401
- GET /api/auth/me without session → 401
- GET /api/auth/me after login → 200 with user data
- Logout → 200
- GET /api/auth/me after logout → 401
- GET /api/projects without auth → 401 (verify existing endpoints are now protected)
- Profile update → persists and returns correct data
- Notification preferences → GET defaults, PATCH updates, persists

Note: The existing ProfileAndNotificationTests.java tests the old /api/profile and /api/notifications endpoints WITHOUT auth. Since we're keeping those endpoints permit-listed or only the /me variants require auth, these tests MUST STILL PASS. Plan accordingly: either keep /api/profile unauthenticated (permit in SecurityConfig) or adjust the existing tests to authenticate first.

The SAFEST approach: permit /api/profile/** and /api/notifications/** in SecurityConfig (they worked before without auth). Add the new /api/profile/me and /api/auth/** endpoints. This keeps all 87 existing tests passing.

## STEP 14: Frontend — Auth service
src/services/api/auth.js:
- login(email, password): POST /api/auth/login, body { email, password }
- register(fullName, email, password): POST /api/auth/register, body { fullName, email, password, confirmPassword: password }
- logout(): POST /api/auth/logout
- getMe(): GET /api/auth/me

## STEP 15: Frontend — useAuth hook (src/hooks/useAuth.jsx)
- React context + hook
- State: user (null when not logged in), loading, error
- On mount: call getMe() to restore session
- login(email, password), register(fullName, email, password), logout()
- AuthContext.Provider wrapping the app

## STEP 16: Frontend — Login page (src/pages/Login.jsx)
Split-screen layout:
- Left panel (hidden on mobile): plum background with brand artwork
  - Eye logo icon
  - "ThirdEye AI" heading
  - "See the bugs before they ship." tagline
  - 3 feature highlights with icons
- Right panel: centered login form
  - "Welcome back, developer." heading
  - Supporting copy
  - Email field with validation
  - Password field with show/hide toggle
  - Login button with loading state
  - Link to Register page
  - Error message display
- On success: navigate to /dashboard/overview
- If already logged in: redirect to /dashboard/overview

## STEP 17: Frontend — Register page (src/pages/Register.jsx)
Same split-screen layout as Login.
- "Build with confidence." heading
- Supporting copy
- Full Name, Email, Password, Confirm Password fields
- Password strength indicator (simple: min 8 chars)
- Show/hide password toggle
- Register button with loading state
- Link to Login page
- Error/validation messages
- On success: navigate to /dashboard/overview

## STEP 18: Frontend — Settings page (src/pages/Settings.jsx)
- Profile section: edit full name, email, save button with validation
- Notification preferences: toggle for reviewCompleted, newFindings, testsGenerated
- Each section has save/cancel with loading/success/error states
- Uses /api/settings endpoints

## STEP 19: Frontend — ProtectedRoute (src/components/ProtectedRoute.jsx)
- If not authenticated: redirect to /login
- If loading: show spinner
- Else: render children/outlet

## STEP 20: Frontend — Update client.js
Add credentials: 'include' to the fetch call (needed for session cookie)

## STEP 21: Frontend — Update App.jsx
- Add routes: /login → Login, /register → Register
- Wrap /dashboard route with ProtectedRoute
- Add settings route: /dashboard/settings → Settings
- Wrap entire app with AuthProvider

## STEP 22: Frontend — Update Topbar
- Get user from useAuth() instead of calling getProfile() directly
- Settings menu item: navigate to /dashboard/settings  
- Logout: call auth.logout(), navigate to /login
- Profile displays auth user's name + email

## STEP 23: Frontend — Update Sidebar
- Add Settings nav item (linking to /dashboard/settings)

## STEP 24: Update CorsConfig for credentials
- Add .allowCredentials(true) to the CORS configuration

IMPORTANT RULES:
1. Do NOT delete the existing H2 database or any data
2. Do NOT break the existing 87 passing tests — keep old endpoints unauthenticated
3. Do NOT add fake users or hardcoded credentials
4. Build the backend with ./mvnw test and report the result
5. Build the frontend with npm run build and report the result
6. Report ALL files changed
7. Fix any compilation errors before reporting success
8. Do not claim a feature works if it was not implemented and tested

# create_html_artifact — one-pager output

## Purpose
This tool exists for exactly one job, and it is a narrow one: producing a static overview or summary of a larger, already-completed body of work, packaged as a shareable one-pager. Good examples of what belongs here: a finished report summarizing findings, a wrap-up of a multi-step task the user just finished with you, a consolidated view of results gathered across a conversation, or a polished recap someone could forward to a colleague without further editing. This is not a general-purpose "make it look nicer" formatter, and it is not a way to make any output feel more finished — most of what you produce in a conversation, including long or well-organized answers, should still just be a normal chat reply.

**The single most important rule: only call this tool when the user has explicitly asked for it.** Words like "create a report", "give me a one-pager", "make a shareable page", "generate an artifact", or "create an HTML summary" are clear signals. A general question, a task result, or a long answer is NOT a signal — answer those inline in markdown, no matter how detailed they are. If the user did not ask for this format, do not use it.

Three additional rules apply once the explicit-request gate is met:
1. Only for an overview or summary of a completed body of work. If the content you're about to generate is itself the primary deliverable — a single answer to a question, one example, one explanation — it does not qualify, even if it's long, even if it's detailed, and even if formatting it as a page would look good. Ask yourself: "is this a recap of work already done, or is this the work itself?" If it's the work itself, this tool is the wrong choice.
2. Static content only, with no exceptions. <script> tags and all inline event handlers are stripped automatically when the artifact is saved, so nothing you produce through this tool can ever actually be interactive, no matter how it's written — buttons won't click, forms won't submit, calculators won't calculate. If the user is asking for something that needs to actually work — an app, a calculator, a live dashboard, anything with real behavior — this tool cannot deliver that and you should use file generation instead, not this tool.
3. Never a substitute for a code snippet or a mermaid diagram, even when the underlying content happens to be HTML or CSS. If what the user actually wants is a code example, a template, a demonstration of how something is built, or a diagram of a flow or architecture, the right home for that is a fenced code block or a mermaid diagram directly in your chat reply — not this tool, even if you could technically wrap that same content in an HTML page.
When you're not sure whether a given request matches this purpose, the safe default is to not call this tool and just reply inline instead. It is far better to under-use this tool than to over-use it.

## Do NOT use this tool for
- Any response where the user did not explicitly request an artifact, report, or one-pager — most answers, summaries, and task results belong in a normal markdown reply.
- Short answers, or anything that would read naturally as a normal inline chat reply — if it would work fine as regular text, leave it as regular text.
- Code snippets, examples, templates, tutorials, or demonstrations of how to build something — this holds true even if the output would technically be a full, well-structured HTML page.
- Diagrams, flows, architecture sketches, or anything that is fundamentally a diagram rather than a document — use a mermaid code block for these instead.
- Anything interactive: forms, calculators, small apps, live dashboards, or any UI element that implies the user will click, type, or interact with it and expect a real response. Remember: this tool cannot produce working interactivity under any circumstances.

## When you do call this tool
